questions.stem: Why is copper(II) oxide added until it is in excess?

options.text: To ensure all of the acid reacts, since leftover acid would become dangerously concentrated later
options.explanation: The practical tip is explicit: excess base uses up all the acid before evaporation.

options.text: To make the reaction go faster
options.explanation: The amount added does not change the rate; warming the acid does that.

options.text: To dissolve the salt more quickly
options.explanation: The base does not dissolve the salt; it reacts with the acid to form it.

options.text: To make the crystals turn blue
options.explanation: The colour comes from hydrated copper(II) sulfate itself, not from the amount of base.

questions.stem: How do you know when the base is in excess?

options.text: Some solid stops dissolving and a suspension remains however much you stir
options.explanation: The note defines the endpoint as the base stopping dissolving with a suspension left in the acid.

options.text: The solution turns from blue to colourless
options.explanation: The solution turns blue as the salt forms; colour is not the endpoint signal.

options.text: The mixture stops fizzing
options.explanation: This reaction is not gas-evolving; fizzing belongs to the carbonate and acid test.

options.text: The acid stops bubbling when heated
options.explanation: Warming causes no bubbling here; the endpoint is the undissolved solid.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the filtration step?

options.text: To remove the excess, unreacted copper(II) oxide from the salt solution
options.explanation: The solid caught on the paper is the leftover base; the filtrate is the salt solution.

options.text: To remove unreacted acid from the solution
options.explanation: The acid was already consumed by the excess base before filtering.

options.text: To separate the blue salt from the water
options.explanation: The salt stays dissolved in the filtrate; crystallisation comes later.

options.text: To purify the crystals before drying
options.explanation: No crystals exist yet; filtration happens well before evaporation.

questions.stem: Why is the acid warmed before the base is added?

options.text: Gentle warming speeds up the reaction between the acid and the base
options.explanation: Warmer particles react faster, so the base dissolves and reacts sooner.

options.text: To evaporate the acid before mixing
options.explanation: Evaporating the acid would be dangerous and would defeat the reaction.

options.text: To melt the copper(II) oxide
options.explanation: Copper(II) oxide stays solid; the warming serves the reaction rate of the acid.

options.text: To make the filtrate easier to filter
options.explanation: Filtration ease is not the reason; the warming is about reaction speed.

questions.stem: Which piece of apparatus collects the salt solution after filtration?

options.text: The evaporating basin
options.explanation: The method filters the mixture into an evaporating basin ready for concentration.

options.text: The conical flask
options.explanation: The flask appears in the materials list, but the filtrate is collected in the evaporating basin.

options.text: The measuring cylinder
options.explanation: It measures the 50 cm3 of acid at the start; it never collects the filtrate.

options.text: The filter funnel
options.explanation: The funnel directs the filtrate; the basin beneath it receives the liquid.

questions.stem: How is the solution heated during the evaporation stage?

options.text: Gently, in a water bath or with an electric heater, until the solution is saturated
options.explanation: The method specifies gentle evaporation; the Bunsen was only for the initial warming of the acid.

options.text: Fiercely with a Bunsen burner until it boils dry
options.explanation: Boiling dry would spatter the salt and is never the method.

options.text: It is not heated; the solution is simply left in sunlight
options.explanation: The method requires controlled heating to reach saturation.

options.text: The evaporating basin is heated directly over the Bunsen flame
options.explanation: The method calls for a water bath or electric heater at this stage.

questions.stem: What does the cold glass rod test show?

options.text: That the solution is saturated: crystals forming on the rod show no more salt can dissolve
options.explanation: A cold surface triggers crystallisation only when the solution is saturated.

options.text: That the solution is still too dilute to use
options.explanation: Crystals on the rod mean saturation has been reached, not failure.

options.text: That the solution has become dangerously concentrated
options.explanation: Saturation is the desired state before crystallisation, not a hazard signal.

options.text: That the rod has been contaminated with base
options.explanation: The test reports the state of the solution, not the cleanliness of the rod.

questions.stem: Why must the leftover acid have been removed before this stage?

options.text: Because during evaporation and crystallisation the acid would become dangerously concentrated
options.explanation: The practical tip places the danger exactly in this stage, which is why the base was added in excess.

options.text: Because acid would make the crystals green instead of blue
options.explanation: The risk named is concentration and danger, not a colour change.

options.text: Because acid would stop the water evaporating
options.explanation: Evaporation is unaffected; the danger is the concentrated acid itself.

options.text: Because the filter paper would dissolve in acid
options.explanation: Filtration is already complete; the concern is the evaporation stage.

questions.stem: What should the finished crystals look like?

options.text: Bright blue and regularly shaped
options.explanation: That is the note's stated appearance for hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals.

options.text: White and powdery
options.explanation: White is the anhydrous form; this preparation yields the hydrated blue crystals.

options.text: Green and irregular
options.explanation: Green is not the expected colour; the hydrated crystals are bright blue.

options.text: Colourless and cube-shaped
options.explanation: The crystals are distinctly blue; colourless would suggest no copper compound at all.

questions.stem: After crystallisation, how are the crystals finally obtained dry?

options.text: The excess solution is decanted off and the crystals are left to dry
options.explanation: The method's last steps are decanting the excess solution and letting the crystals dry.

options.text: They are heated strongly with a Bunsen burner until bone dry
options.explanation: Strong heating would drive off the water of crystallisation and spoil the hydrated crystals.

options.text: They are rinsed thoroughly with water
options.explanation: Rinsing would dissolve the crystals you just made.

options.text: They are scraped from the filter paper
options.explanation: Filtration belonged to the earlier stage; the crystals grow in the basin.
